title: From AI Feedback to Intellectual Friction: What AI Should Do in the Writing Classroom
author: Tom Daccord
summary: Tom Daccord uses Stanford's SCALE report on highly active MagicSchool users to show that English teachers lean heavily on AI feedback tools, with 45% of ELA educators using the Writing Feedback tool against 17% of others. He values the report for observing what teachers actually do, but notes it cannot say whether the feedback was pedagogically effective or whether students acted on it. That gap leads to his central question, whether AI help in responding to writing helps students become better writers. He describes two designs that keep intellectual work with students: the PAIRR process from UC Davis, where students exchange peer feedback, receive targeted AI feedback, must ask at least two follow-up questions and then decide how to revise, and John Dolman's Opposing Counsel chatbots, which challenge students' rhetorical arguments without supplying them. His conclusion is that the aim is to match the type and intensity of AI support to student need, and to ask what intellectual responsibility students retain after feedback arrives.
points: English teachers cluster around AI feedback tools, and 45% of ELA educators in the SCALE sample used MagicSchool's Writing Feedback tool versus 17% of non-ELA educators.
Platform activity data shows what teachers do but not whether AI feedback improved student writing, which is the unanswered question.
PAIRR keeps feedback targeted to a few priorities and requires students to question the AI and weigh it against peer feedback before revising.
In Dolman's Opposing Counsel task, chatbots supply the challenge but not the argument, and the experience showed that too much friction or coaching can backfire.
Effective practice means deliberately deciding when AI should assist, guide or challenge, so that students keep the pivotal decisions.
quotes: The Writing Feedback tool offers a more structured approach, with fields for the assignment description, grade level, student work, and an optional rubric. It’s convenient and seemingly well aligned with an important teaching task.

While observing platform activity is revealing (and more evidential than pronouncements), it alone does not directly measure pedagogical quality or student learning. We don’t know whether the generated feedback is pedagogically effective or whether students acted on it.
The SCALE report findings therefore expose a consequential question. AI can assist teachers to respond to student writing, but does that assistance help students become better writers?

PAIRR is a five-stage process: Students first write a draft, exchange peer feedback, receive AI feedback, evaluate both sources, and revise. The AI is explicitly instructed to provide feedback that helps students improve their writing without doing the writing for them.

AI feedback was not simply more feedback, piled on top of human feedback. It created opportunities for students to evaluate varied perspectives and exercise independent judgment about their revisions. It indicates that learning opportunities lie not only in receiving feedback but also in deciding what to do with it.

Dolman’s experience points out that less can be more. Some students thought the bots offered too much coaching; others found them too combative. Providing students with more intellectual friction does not necessarily translate into more learning.
The goal isn’t to maximize or minimize AI feedback. It is to find the right balance and match the type and intensity of AI support to the student’s needs and the instructional goal.
The ultimate goal isn’t to improve the paper the student is currently writing. It’s to help students become better thinkers and writers.
